food.text: Stroganina is a dish of the northern Russians and the indigenous people of northern Arctic Siberia. It is made of raw, thin, long-sliced frozen fish. It is popular with native Siberians and appears in Yakutian, Eskimo, Komi and Yamal cuisines.
In 1985 Greenland left the European Economic Community. It did not agree with the EEC's commercial fishing regulations, and it objected to an EEC ban on sealskin products.
Traditional stroganina is made with freshwater whitefish salmonids found in the Siberian Arctic waters, such as nelma, muksun, chir and omul. Only rarely is it made with sturgeon.

The fish for stroganina is usually caught by ice fishing during the late fall and fresh frozen to avoid ice crystals forming in the meat. It can be glazed with near-freezing ice water to prevent dehydration. The fish is typically frozen straight, without bending its body.

Greenlanders have historically moved in search of resources such as seals and cod. Climate change and the decline of fish stocks are now changing the livelihood of the Greenlandic population, particularly the Greenlandic Inuit. Among the Tunumiit Inuit of east Greenland, many traditional hunters are shifting to tourism because they can no longer provide for their families through traditional hunting, and smaller villages that rely on hunting and fishing fear climate change will contribute to the end of their traditional lifestyles.

To keep stroganina frozen as long as possible, it is served immediately on non-metallic frozen plates or in ice-cold bowls, with salt and black pepper powder. It is usually eaten with the hands while still frozen.
Stroganina goes by different names and fish in different places. Around Lake Baikal it is called raskolotka, and in Kaliningrad it is made with Sarda.
Stroganina, whose name literally means "shavings", is cut from frozen fish with a Yakutian knife. The knife's geometry is best suited to cutting long slices that form ribbon curls.

art.text: Inuit artists historically preferred walrus ivory as their medium. Since southern markets for Inuit art were established in 1945, prints and figurative carvings in relatively soft stone such as soapstone, serpentinite or argillite have also become popular.

The Winnipeg Art Gallery holds the largest public collection of contemporary Inuit art in the world. In 2007 the Museum of Inuit Art opened in Toronto, but it closed in 2016 because of a lack of resources.

Modern Inuit art developed in the latter half of the 20th century, as Indigenous peoples of the Canadian Arctic began living in fixed communities in the late 1940s. As artists multiplied and the Canadian government promoted stone carving, contemporary Inuit art grew popular in Canada and abroad.

Since the establishment of southern markets for Inuit art in 1945, prints and figurative carvings in soft stone such as soapstone have become popular alongside the traditional medium of walrus ivory. The Winnipeg Art Gallery holds the largest public collection of contemporary Inuit art in the world.

Around 1949, many Inuit were forcibly moved into settled communities, and the Canadian government began encouraging a carving industry as a source of income. Inuit art then changed markedly in size, media, motif and style from what it had been before.

In 1951, James Houston encouraged Inuit in Kinngait to produce stone carvings. It was mostly men who took up carving, and Ovilu Tunnillie was one of the few women to work in sculpture and earn a national reputation.

The Government of Canada's encouragement of commercial carving was initially heavy-handed. This is most clearly shown by the pamphlet "Eskimo Handicrafts", circulated among Inuit communities in the early 1950s to inspire Inuit sculptors. It pictured artifacts from the Canadian Museum of Civilization, and many of them, such as totem poles, were not germane to Inuit culture.

The first generation of Inuit artists in Kinngait sold their carvings in the 1940s and 1950s to the Baffin Trading Company (1939–1946) and the Hudson's Bay Company. The West Baffin Eskimo Cooperative was founded there in 1959 and became the primary purchaser of arts and crafts.

Inuvialuk artist Floyd Kuptana was born in 1964 near the Distant Early Warning Line station at Cape Parry. He began by sanding and polishing carvings for his cousins Francis and Abraham Anghik Ruben, then apprenticed with David Ruben Piqtoukun and made his own work after leaving in 1992.

Inuit carvers still work almost entirely by hand, preferring an axe and file to power tools for greater control over the stone. The last stage is hours of rubbing with several grades of waterproof sandpaper, and some stone is orange-red and imported from Brazil.
Library and Archives Canada acquired Floyd Kuptana's "Self-portrait by Floyd Kuptana" in 2007. It later appeared in a 2018 joint exhibit at the Glenbow art and history museum in Calgary.

war.text: Between August 1941 and May 1945, 78 Arctic convoys sailed from the United Kingdom, Iceland and North America, mostly to Arkhangelsk and Murmansk in the northern Soviet Union. About 1,400 merchant ships took part, mainly escorted by the Royal Navy. The convoys lost 85 merchant vessels and 16 British warships.
war.source_title: Arctic convoys of World War II

war.text: After Denmark fell to Nazi Germany in April 1940, Greenland was left as an unoccupied territory of an occupied nation. The United States, still neutral, firmly rejected "third party" intervention there. From 1941 until 1945 it built air and sea facilities, radio and weather stations, ports and search-and-rescue stations on the island.

The Petsamo–Kirkenes offensive of 1944 was the last major offensive fought in an Arctic environment. The Red Army drove the Wehrmacht back into Norway and seized the nickel mines of Petsamo. Because of this, the Soviet Army studied it intensively afterward.

The Arctic Star campaign medal was instituted by the United Kingdom on 19 December 2012 for those who served on the Arctic Convoys. It came more than sixty-seven years after the war ended, following a 16-year campaign by veterans. They stressed that Arctic service differed from that in the Atlantic, a journey Winston Churchill called "the worst journey in the world".

The Battle of the Barents Sea saw a strong German naval force fail to defeat a British escort of cruisers and destroyers guarding Convoy JW 51B. The failure infuriated Hitler and led to a strategic change from surface raiders to submarines. Some capital ships were dismantled and their armament used in coastal defences.
war.source_title: Arctic convoys of World War II

war.text: The German battleship Tirpitz spent most of the war in Norwegian fjords, apart from an abortive attempt to attack Convoy PQ 12 in March 1942 and a raid on Spitzbergen in September 1943. After being attacked and damaged several times, it was sunk in Tromsø fjord on 12 November 1944 by the Royal Air Force.
war.source_title: Arctic convoys of World War II

war.text: When the United States entered the war on 11 December 1941, Greenland became a warring nation. Contact with Copenhagen was broken off, rationing and daylight saving time were introduced, and local currency and stamps were printed. In 1942 combat patrols began flying from Bluie West One, headquarters of the Coast Guard Greenland Patrol.

Arctic convoys carried food and munitions to the besieged city of Leningrad by trains, barges and trucks from 1941. Many supplies were destroyed en route by the Luftwaffe and by Naval Detachment K. Even so, convoys continued to deliver food in 1942, 1943 and 1944.
war.source_title: Arctic convoys of World War II

war.text: On 11 March 1943, a Sledge Patrol team discovered the German weather station Holzauge at Hansa Bay on Sabine Island. The Germans realized they had been discovered and gave chase, and the team had to abandon their equipment, including their dog teams, and retreat to the station at Eskimonæs to warn Ib Poulsen, the patrol commander. Poulsen reported the base on 13 March, and Governor Brun designated the patrol the "Army of Greenland" with Poulsen as its captain. On 26 March the Germans ambushed Corporal Eli Knudsen at Sandodden and killed him with a machine-gun burst meant for his dogs; he was the patrol's only casualty of the war.

For the 1944 Petsamo–Kirkenes offensive, the Soviets fielded 126th and 127th Rifle Corps of light infantry with ski troops and naval infantry. They also had numerous horse- and reindeer-equipped transportation companies and two battalions with US-supplied amphibious vehicles. Against 110 Soviet tanks, the Germans lacked any armour.

Håkon Nilsen served as torpedo commander on HNoMS Stord and took part in 20 Arctic convoys as well as the Normandy landings. On 28 September 2014 he became the first and only Norwegian war veteran to be awarded the Arctic Star posthumously.

literature.text: Barry Lopez's 1986 book Arctic Dreams explores the Arctic landscape, its wildlife, and the relationship between people and the natural world. It won the National Book Award for Nonfiction and was a National Book Critics Circle Award finalist.

Greenland's national anthem, "Nunarput, utoqqarsuanngoravit", has lyrics written in 1912 by the pastor and poet Henrik Lund. It was set to music by Jonathan Petersen and adopted as the national anthem in 1916.

Hugh Montgomery's The Voyage of the Arctic Tern is a children's verse novel about an ancient ship and its captain, Bruno, who seeks redemption because he has been cursed with eternal life. In the story, Bruno betrays his fellow villagers to marauders led by the "Mad Dog", and everyone else in the village dies as a result. Guilt-ridden, he tries to drown himself, but the ghosts of the dead villagers stop him and curse him to sail forever unless he completes three tasks. Illustrated by Nick Poullis, it was published in 2002 by Candlewick Press and Walker Books.
literature.source_title: The Voyage of the Arctic Tern
tags: The Voyage of the Arctic Tern

literature.text: Modern Greenlandic literature began in 1914 with the publication of the first Greenlandic novel, Singnagtugaĸ ("A Dream"), by Mathias Storch. It presents a utopian vision of a future, free Greenland.

Michiko Kakutani wrote in The New York Times that Arctic Dreams is a book about the Arctic North in the way that Moby-Dick is a novel about whales. Robert Macfarlane, in The Guardian, called Barry Lopez "the most important living writer about wilderness".
Henrik Lund was a Greenlandic lyricist, painter, and Lutheran pastor born in Nanortalik in 1875. He composed hymns in the Greenlandic language, which were published in 1909, 1930, 1937, and 1945.

Before writing Arctic Dreams, Barry Lopez spent five years working as a field biologist in the Canadian Arctic. He knew places from Melville Island and the Hood River to Baffin Bay and the Beaufort Sea, and his writing combines scientific observation with literary sensitivity.

Henrik Lund's poem "Igdlugssaq Nápagaungmat", or "When the House Was Built", describes the seemingly minor event of constructing a home in Angmagssalik. While not overtly heroic, the act is presented as useful and as a demonstration of community affection.

Hugh Montgomery began The Voyage of the Arctic Tern as a Christmas present for his godchildren in 1993, and it took him three years to finish. After many publishers rejected it, he self-published it, and all 2,000 first copies sold. It won Book of the Year and Poetry Book of the Year at the 2000 David St John Thomas Charitable Trust Self-Publishing Awards.
literature.source_title: The Voyage of the Arctic Tern
tags: The Voyage of the Arctic Tern
David St John Thomas Charitable Trust

literature.text: Augo Lynge's Ukiut 300-nngornerat ("Three Hundred Years Later", 1931) presented a utopian vision of a future, free Greenland. Like Storch's earlier novel, it imagined a Greenland that governed itself.

From the 1970s onward, a strongly politicised postcolonial literary movement emerged in Greenland. Greenlandic literature increasingly addressed colonisation, cultural identity and political autonomy, with figures such as Hans Anthon Lynge and Ole Korneliussen.

Inuit legends and myths in Greenland were preserved orally before a written tradition existed. In the early 20th century Knud Rasmussen collected them in northern Greenland, following Hinrich Johannes Rink's earlier work in the west.

Arctic Dreams presents the concept of "Isumataq", which holds that no individual can possess all knowledge, so people must share information and combine their experience. Lopez argues that Indigenous knowledge is essential to understanding and surviving in the Arctic. The book also describes the mistreatment of Inuit people by explorers such as Robert Peary.

Lund's father, Isak Lund, was a head catechist and a poet whose patriotic sentiments show in works such as "Nuna Tassa Tupingnartoq", or "This Is a Wonderful Country". Henrik Lund learned to love music and poetry through his family and a local German Moravian mission.

science.text: The Greenland ice sheet is the second-largest body of ice in the world, covering around 80% of Greenland's surface. It averages 1,673 metres thick and is over 3,488 metres thick at its maximum. Scientists now find it is losing ice at the fastest rate in at least the past 12,000 years.

Since the middle of the 20th century, the Arctic has been warming at about twice the global rate. Rising temperatures put pressure on plant and tree species and contribute to Greenland's melting ice sheet. The melting ice is also revealing minerals, oil and gas, which has attracted investors.

In 2021, rain fell at Greenland's highest point for the first time in recorded history. The event was so unexpected that the research station at the summit had no rain gauges for the occasion. It came during one of the massive melting events, when practically the entire ice sheet surface was melting.

The International Arctic Science Committee was founded in 1990 by representatives of national scientific organizations of the eight Arctic countries. Its founding articles were signed in Resolute Bay, Canada. Its membership today includes 25 countries, 17 of them non-Arctic.

The Greenland ice sheet always lost some mass through calving, but snowfall used to balance it. Greenland has been warming since around 1900, and from the 1980s the losses became larger than the gains. After 1996, Greenland has not had a single year when it did not lose ice mass on average.

Jacobshavn Isbræ in west Greenland is the ice sheet's single largest outlet glacier, and glaciologists have observed it for many decades. Its flow speed almost doubled between 1997 and 2003 as the ice tongue in front of it disintegrated. It reached 45 metres per day in 2012, then slowed and showed mass gain between 2016 and 2019.

China's Yellow River Station was established in 2004 in Norway's Svalbard archipelago. It has conducted studies in geology, atmosphere and space physics. China also began operating research icebreakers in 1999, including the Xue Long and Xue Long 2.

Northern Greenland's Petermann Glacier has degraded rapidly in recent decades. In August 2010 a 260 square kilometre iceberg calved from its ice shelf, the largest Arctic iceberg since 1962. Another iceberg, twice the area of Manhattan, broke off in July 2012.

In 2009 the Greenland Climate Research Centre was set up in Nuuk, funded by a DKK 35 million grant from the Danish Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation. It studies how climate change affects Greenland and the Arctic, and the consequences for nature and society. It is linked to the Greenland Institute of Natural Resources and the University of Greenland, Ilisimatusarfik.

The International Arctic Science Committee coordinated the Fourth International Conference on Arctic Research Planning, a process running from 2022 to 2026. Its final outcomes were released in Aarhus, Denmark, on 26 March 2026. The reports are intended to inform preparations for the Fifth International Polar Year, with intensive observation planned for 2032 to 2033.

The China-Iceland Arctic Science Observatory opened on October 18, 2018, in Kárhóll, northern Iceland. It studies the aurora borealis and upper atmosphere, and its outdoor field holds a rio-meter with 37 antennas. It is jointly operated by the Polar Research Institute of China and the Icelandic Centre for Research.

The Vinland Map came to light in 1957 and was presented in 1965 as a genuine pre-Columbian map. Later chemical analyses identified a major ink ingredient as a 20th-century artificial pigment. In 2018, specialists at Yale declared it conclusively a modern forgery.

politics.text: When Nazi Germany occupied Denmark in April 1940, Greenland became an unoccupied territory of an occupied nation. The United Kingdom, United States or Canada might have seized it. Instead, the island ended up under American protection.

Arctic exploration put Danish sovereignty over all of Greenland in doubt, since the principle of terra nullius seemed to leave large tracts open to newcomers. Norway claimed Erik the Red's Land in eastern Greenland in 1931. The Permanent Court of International Justice ruled against Norway two years later, supporting Danish sovereignty.
In 1953, Greenland's colonial status ended and it became an integral part of the Kingdom of Denmark, with representation in the Folketing. In 1979 the Folketing granted the island home rule.

Greenland's two sheriffs, Eske Brun and Aksel Svane, invoked an emergency clause of a 1925 law and declared Greenland a self-ruling territory. They believed this was best for the colony while Denmark was occupied by Nazi Germany.
In 2009, all matters other than defense and foreign policy were transferred to Greenland's regional parliament. This was the further step after home rule was granted in 1979.

The American presence in Greenland continued in decreasing numbers after the war, until the Kauffmann-Hull agreement was replaced by a new base treaty in 1951. The wartime experience of an independent Greenland led to a dramatic restructuring and modernization of Danish policy toward the colony.

Danish ambassador Henrik Kauffmann made an agreement 'in the name of the king' with the United States after the German occupation of Denmark on 9 April 1940. It authorized the United States to defend the Danish colonies on Greenland from German aggression.
politics.source_title: History of the Jews in Greenland

politics.text: After Germany's defeat, Greenlanders celebrated the liberation of Denmark in Nuuk on 5 May 1945. Eske Brun's administration surrendered its emergency powers to Copenhagen. Treason charges against Kauffmann were dropped, and the Danish parliament ratified his agreement with the United States.

The Three-year Expedition to East Greenland ran from 1931 to 1934 and was led by Lauge Koch. It was financed by the Carlsberg Foundation and the Danish state. The state's involvement had political connotations because of the ongoing dispute between Denmark and Norway over East Greenland.

The self-rule declaration was coordinated with Ambassador Henrik Kauffmann and the U.S. State Department. It fit the American declaration of 1920 that no third nation would necessarily be accepted as a sovereign in Greenland. This stance was seen as an extension of the Monroe Doctrine.
The US air base built at Thule in 1941 was renamed Pituffik Space Base in 2023. It is now used as a base for space exploration.
politics.source_title: History of the Jews in Greenland

philosophy.text: Inuit were first exposed to Christian Europeans in the 16th century. Over the following centuries, missionaries worked to convert Inuit communities, and by the mid-20th century most Inuit had formally converted to Christianity. This led to a substantial decline in the angakut, the ritual specialists of the older tradition.

Traditional Inuit belief holds that a human has two souls, one of which can leave the body at night, and that a prolonged absence of this free soul can result in bodily death. Ritual specialists called angakut mediated between people and spirits, performing rituals for healing, recovering lost objects, or helping the hunt. They were both respected and feared, since they were deemed capable of using their spirits to harm as well as heal, and were often thought able to steal all or part of a person's soul.

By the mid-20th century most Inuit had formally converted to Christianity, which sharply reduced the role of the angakut and other Inuit traditions. From the 1970s, a renewed movement arose to celebrate traditional Inuit culture and encourage Inuit pride.

Inuit religion has no formal leadership or organizational structure and shows much internal variation. In 1991, Merkur described it as varyingly extinct, obsolescent and persisting, depending on the community.

Among the Inughuit of northwest Greenland, everyone was baptized by 1934 and the angakut were extinct by the mid-20th century. In eastern Greenland, the angakut kept working, largely unhindered by Christianity, until the early 20th century.

Ethnographic accounts from the Inughuit and Labrador Inuit describe a recurring belief that ghosts and spirits may visit a person through dreams. Dreams are generally deemed religiously significant, and sometimes have a prophetic quality.

In 1975 the Inuit Cultural Institute launched, as a pan-Inuit ideology fostered growing appreciation of old traditions. The 1999 founding of the Nunavut government in Canada further assisted research into traditional Inuit culture.

Catholic priests have visited Greenland since 1930, after Bishop Theodore Suhr of Copenhagen received Vatican permission to ask the Missionary Oblates of Mary Immaculate to missionize there. In 1980 the Little Sisters of Jesus established a fraternity in Nuuk with three sisters.

In fall 1942, Rabbi Julius Amos Leibert, a U.S. Army chaplain, conducted High Holiday services in Greenland, Labrador and Iceland. Jewish servicemen in Greenland received chaplain visits during World War II, supported by the National Jewish Welfare Board.
philosophy.source_title: History of the Jews in Greenland

philosophy.text: Nurse Rita Scheftelowitz moved from Denmark to Greenland for adventure and lived an Orthodox Jewish life there, met by a visiting journalist in Aasiaat. She managed to eat kosher by avoiding meat and eating the plentiful local fish.
philosophy.source_title: History of the Jews in Greenland

philosophy.text: Since 2001, Paul Cohen has been the sole Jewish resident of Greenland, living in Narsaq and working as a translator. Despite his remoteness, he says Jewish tourists are always able to find him.
philosophy.source_title: History of the Jews in Greenland

culture.text: Inuit religion has no formal leadership and includes ritual specialists called angakut, who mediated between people and spirits. By the mid-20th century most Inuit had formally converted to Christianity, and the angakut and many traditions declined sharply. From the 1970s a renewed movement celebrated traditional Inuit culture and encouraged Inuit pride.

Greenland's rapid change from a hunter-gatherer to a post-industrial society in the 20th century drove a demographic transition and a significant population increase. Danish authorities responded in the 1960s and 70s with a highly controversial IUD program, known as the Spiral case. At least 4,500 Inuit women were implanted with IUDs, about half the fertile women at the time, and it is unclear how many cases lacked consent or proper explanation. Danish doctors wrote openly of the program in journals, and the involuntary program regained public awareness in 2022 with an investigation.

In Greenland, most people are Christian and belong to the Church of Greenland, which is Lutheran in orientation. Traditional Inuit spiritual beliefs nonetheless remain strong in many remote communities.
State-enforced Lutheranism stayed in place in Greenland until 1953, when religious liberty was declared. In the 20th century a small permanent Catholic presence was re-established there.

In Greenland, state-enforced Lutheranism stayed in place until 1953, when religious liberty was declared. Before that, the Church of Denmark, the established church, had shaped religious life there. Traditional Inuit spiritual beliefs nonetheless remain strong in many of Greenland's remote communities.

The first translation of the whole Bible into Greenlandic was not completed until 1900, though the New Testament had been translated piecemeal since the first settlement on Kangeq Island. An improved translation using the modern orthography was completed in 2000.

On 21 June 2009, the Church of Greenland was taken over by the local government of Greenland, which now handles its funding and legislation. It is nonetheless still a diocese of the Church of Denmark. It followed the Church of the Faroe Islands, which became independent in July 2007.

On 21 June 2009, the Church of Greenland was taken over by Greenland's local government, so its funding and legislation now fall under that government. It remains a diocese of the Church of Denmark. It followed the example of the Church of the Faroe Islands, which became fully independent in 2007.

Vivian Motzfeldt moved to a boarding school in Qaqortoq at age seven. Each Christmas she and her siblings returned to their hometown of Upernaviarsuk, and she spent Christmas at her childhood home until she was 17. She later studied the cultural and social history of Greenland at the University of Greenland.

In summer 1980 the Little Sisters of Jesus set up a fraternity in Nuuk with three sisters. In 2007 a global environmental summit was held at their Catholic church there. It was attended by Catholic, Orthodox and United Nations officials, with the approval of Pope Benedict XVI.
